Senator Grohoski, friends and colleagues on the Joint Standing Committee on Taxation, I am
Dan Sayre, the Representative for House District 135, the greater part of the town of Kennebunk.
I present for your consideration LD 714, An Act to Amend the Tax Laws.
This bill has been retitled "An Act to Prevent State Income Tax from Being Collected on
Money Stolen from Victims of Scams." It addresses the rising problem of scams that induce
older Mainers to liquidate retirement assets and deposit them in untraceable accounts, resulting
in unrecoverable loss.
The FBI tracks financial scams targeting seniors, including investment scams, technical/customer support schemes, money mule and romance scams, and others. According to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) data, in 2024 there was a total of $4.885 billion in losses from
147,127 complaints nationwide. This is a 46% increase in complaints from 2023, as well as a 43% increase in losses. The FBI reported that in Maine 608 victims lost nearly $13 million.
These scams take many forms, but a common approach is to convince retirees with substantial
savings that the scammers are agents of the federal government. They persuade their victims to turn over their funds either to safeguard them or to assist in a (fraudulent) investigation of malicious actors. Once transferred, the funds disappear, but the citizen is stuck with federal and state tax obligations as a result of having taken distributions from their retirement accounts.
The federal tax code allows this sort of loss to be deducted from income. Maine state law does not. This bill aims to correct that. To be specific, the federal internal revenue code provides that a taxpayer can reduce their tax liability for such losses under Code Section 165. This bill would extend that same remedy for Mainers' state tax obligations if they are victimized by a scam.
Please note that the bill is currently drafted to take effect for tax years beginning January 1,
2026. I ask that it be amended to January 1, 2025. Several Maine families suffered substantial

losses to scammers in tax year 2025, and I believe some are present to testify today. I want this
bill to help them.
Thank you for your time and consideration. I will endeavor to answer any questions you have,
but I believe representatives of Maine Revenue Services are present who can speak with more
expertise regarding the details of the federal and state tax codes and the specifics of making this
change.

10061799:
Testimony in Support of LD 714: "An Act to Prevent State Income Tax from Being Collected on Money Stolen from
Victims of Scams "
Senator Grohoski, Representative Sayre, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Taxation, my name is Montana Towers, and I serve as policy analyst for Maine Policy Institute. Maine Policy is a free market think tank, a nonpartisan, nonprofit organization that advocates for individual liberty and economic freedom in Maine. Thank you for the opportunity to submit testimony in support of LD 714, "An Act to Prevent State Income Tax from Being Collected on Money Stolen from Victims of Scams."
This bill mirrors the federal theft-loss deduction available under federal law and makes it so that Maine taxpayers who claim a legitimate scam-related loss at the federal level will no longer face state income tax on the same stolen funds. This common sense conformity delivers immediate relief to victims already reeling from financial harm and prevents the state from effectively taxing money that victims no longer possess.
A Welcome but Incomplete Step
While MPI supports broader tax conformity overall, adopting the federal scam-loss deduction is especially valuable because it directly protects vulnerable Mainers, often seniors or working families, who have already suffered devastating financial harm through no fault of their own. Without this change, the state would compound the injury by taxing phantom income that victims no longer possess, effectively turning a crime into an extra tax bill.
While we applaud this bill for closing a narrow but painful gap in current law, it also illustrates the deeper problem that Maine's tax code remains only partially conformed to federal provisions. Because Maine has not adopted full conformity with the federal tax code, state lawmakers are forced to chase behind every federal change with one-off bills like this one. The result is complexity, uncertainty, and higher compliance costs for everyday Mainers. A small, single issue solution, no matter how well intentioned, cannot substitute for systematic alignment.
The Need for More Tax Conformity
Full conformity with the federal tax code is therefore the best way forward. Conforming would simplify compliance, reduce administrative burdens, and create a more stable and predictable tax environment for Maine taxpayers. When state tax policy diverges significantly from federal law, individuals and businesses are forced to navigate two

separate systems, increasing paperwork, confusion, and the likelihood of costly filing errors. These unnecessary complications place a disproportionate burden on small businesses and working families who often lack the time and resources to manage complex tax requirements.
Bringing Maine's tax code into closer alignment with the federal code would streamline the filing process, reduce compliance costs, and improve transparency for taxpayers. A simpler and more consistent tax structure allows businesses to spend less time dealing with regulatory hurdles and more time investing, hiring, and expanding operations in Maine. At a time when our state must remain competitive with neighboring states for jobs, investment, and population growth, reducing unnecessary tax complexity is a commonsense reform.
Federal conformity does not mean relinquishing state control over tax policy. Rather, it represents a practical step toward a simpler, more efficient system that respects taxpayers' time and resources while promoting economic growth. By reducing duplication and aligning definitions and calculations with federal standards, Maine can make its tax code more accessible, predictable, and supportive of long-term economic prosperity.
For these reasons, Maine Policy Institute strongly urges this committee to vote "Ought to Pass" on LD 714. Thank you for your time and consideration.

Chair, Vice Chair, and members of the Taxation Committee, thank you for the opportunity to speak today. My name is Phil Nadeau, and I have lived in Maine for sixty years. I am here as a resident and as someone who was preparing for retirement but can no longer do so because I became a victim of a pig-butchering investment scam.
Eight weeks was all it took for criminals to dismantle the financial security I had spent 40 plus years building. The scam began on Facebook, where someone approached me in what seemed like a normal, friendly interaction. Over time, that person built trust, created a sense of legitimacy, and eventually guided me into what I believed was a real investment opportunity. The platform they directed me to showed detailed account balances, profits, and tax obligations; The investment strategy was even tested for validation by using a much smaller sum of money. Everything appeared professional and authentic. In reality, every dollar I sent was stolen the moment it left my account.
By the time I realized what had happened, I had lost $960,000.00 (nine hundred and sixty thousand dollars). That number is difficult to say out loud. It represents my retirement, my plans, and the stability I had worked for over four decades. The emotional impact was profound; Shame, disbelief, and the overwhelming fear of being judged for something I did not understand was a crime until it was too late.
The IRS now recognizes pig-butchering scams as a form of investment theft. Under the updated interpretation of IRC �165, these losses qualify as theft losses, meaning victims may deduct the full amount of their loss when it is clear the funds are gone and unrecoverable. This recognition is important, because it acknowledges that victims are not making reckless investment choices; but instead are being targeted and deceived by sophisticated criminal networks.
The State of Maine has not yet made the same recognition and that leaves people, like me, exposed to state-level tax obligations on income never actually received.
That is why this bill matters. It ensures that Maine residents who fall victim to these crimes are not taxed on monies that have been stolen through fraudulent investment scams. It prevents victims from being financially punished a second time. And it brings Maine's tax policy in line with the realities of modern cybercrime that is organized, international, and designed to exploit trust.
In my case, preliminary numbers calculated by my CPA, are that I will incur a tax bill in excess of $80,000.00 (eighty thousand dollars). I no longer have that money available because it was stolen and I will be at the mercy of the MRS to develop a repayment plan. If provided with the proposed tax abatement and combined with the fact that I will work an extra 7 (seven) to 10 (ten)

years, I may be able to recreate a reasonable portfolio. Being required to pay this state tax obligation will most certainly eliminate that possibility from happening. As sad as it sounds it may put me in a position where I need to ask the state for assistance at that time. I cannot recover what I lost. But the state can prevent further harm. This bill offers fairness, clarity, and compassion to people who have already endured life-altering financial and emotional trauma. I respectfully urge the Committee to support it. Thank you for your time and for your commitment to protecting Maine residents.
Respectfully Philip J. Nadeau Maine Resident

Showing that kind of familiarity is a prime feature of the scammer's
playbook, much like a psychic demonstrates personal knowledge in front of a large audience, said Dan Simons, a psychology professor at the University of Illinois Urbana-Charnpaign. He and Christopher Chabris, a cognitive
scientist, co-authored a book on scams, "Nobody's Fool: Why We Get Taken In and What We Can Do About It."
"There "s a lot of information online that's available to everyone," Simons
said. "(The scammer) was probably on Google Maps and could see the area. They give you just enough information to make it sound like they know
things about you."

Simonssaid most cyber scams are run by international crime syndicates from call centers in places like Myanmar, Pakistan and India. Often they're
staffed by victims of human trafficking who have no choice in the matter.
Most scammers also have a virtual script based on a lot of trial and error,
Simons said. They're happy when someone suspects it's a scam and hangs
up because they don't Want to waste time.
